reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Isaiah sat in his car seat. "Let's play the shout game," said Dad. "I say a word. You shout the opposite."

Dad said, "Big." Isaiah shouted, "Small!" A big truck went by. Then a small car went by. "Look, small!" said Isaiah.

Dad said, "Hot." Isaiah touched the warm vent near his feet. "Ooh, hot," he said. Then he touched his cold cup. There was ice inside. "Cold!" he shouted. "I win!" said Isaiah.

Dad said, "Fast." The car zoomed down the big road. Then the car stopped at a light. A little turtle crossed in front of them. It was so slow. "Slow!" laughed Isaiah. "The turtle is slow!"

Then Dad said, "Up." Isaiah thought and thought. He pointed at his shoe. "Down!" he said.

Just then the light turned green. The turtle was safe on the grass. Dad drove on. "One more," said Isaiah. "Say night."

"Night," said Dad.

"Day!" Isaiah shouted, and the sun peeked out from a cloud.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Raphael sat in the big chair at the dentist. The dentist had a friendly smile. She showed Raphael her tiny mirror. She wanted to look at his teeth.

"I want to see clean teeth," she said. Raphael had eaten lunch before he came. He had used the toilet too. Then he had skipped straight to the toys. His hands were still sticky.

The dentist looked at his hands. Raphael looked too. He saw the sticky fingers. He jumped down from the chair. He ran to the sink. He pumped the soap. He rubbed and rubbed. The bubbles grew big. He counted to twenty with the nurse. The water washed the bubbles away. His hands were clean now.

Raphael skipped back to the big chair. He held up his hands. The dentist looked at his shiny fingers and his shiny teeth. "All clean," she said. She gave him a sticker with a star on it. Raphael stuck it right in the middle of his shirt. "Next time, I will wash first," he told the nurse. She laughed and gave him a high five.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
The school bus was big and yellow. Eva held her mama's hand. She climbed the steps all by herself. She sat by the window. She saw a pink backpack on the seat across from her. A boy rubbed his nose. He looked a little sleepy.

The bus went bump, bump, bump. Eva counted the seats. One, two, three, four. Then the bus stopped. It was school.

The teacher took the class outside. There was a slide. Eva ran to it fast. She went down once. "Again!" she said. She ran to the front. But other children stood in a line. Eva stood at the back. One child went down. Then one more. Then it was Eva's turn. She slid down and laughed. The line moved like that, one by one. At story time, Eva got to write her own name on a paper. Then the boy from the bus sat next to her. "You kept going down," he said. "You waited so well," said the teacher. Eva smiled and got back in line.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Arlo sat at the big table. He had paper and markers. He wanted to make a garden. First he drew one green stem. Then two green stems. Then three green stems.

Arlo grabbed the red marker. He pressed too hard. The marker jumped! It made a red line on his hand. Arlo looked at his hand. "Oh no," he said. The red mark would not rub off on the dry paper.

Mom came over. "Let's go to the sink," she said. She turned on the water. It was warm, not hot. She gave Arlo the soap. The soap felt slippery. Arlo rubbed and rubbed. The red mark began to fade. Then it was gone! His hand was clean again.

Arlo went back to the table. He drew his garden again. Red flowers, yellow flowers, blue flowers. He held up his hand and smiled. "All clean," he said. Then he drew one more flower, just for Mom.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story: Avery sat at the little table at school. It was snow day. Big flakes fell past the window. "Look, the snow!" said her friend Milo. Avery wanted to paint the snow. She got white paper. She got white paint. She made a stroke. It did not show. White on white was hard to see. Avery tipped her cup. Paint began to spill. "Be careful," said Teacher Jo. "I see the snow!" said Avery. Milo leaned close. "It looks soft like my pet bunny," he said. Avery painted one more soft white hill.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Elizabeth stood at the classroom door. Her tummy felt fluttery, like little birds inside. She held her mommy's hand very tight.

"Your tummy feels funny?" Mommy asked. Elizabeth nodded. "My tummy felt that way on my first day too," said Mommy. "It is okay to feel this way." Elizabeth looked up. Mommy had felt fluttery too? She took a big breath. Then she let go of Mommy's hand and stepped inside.

A boy sat at a table. He was pulling on his coat zipper. It was stuck. His face looked worried. Elizabeth knew stuck zippers. She walked over and held the coat flat. The zipper slid down easy. The boy smiled. "Thank you," he said.

The teacher brought a box. Inside was a green toy frog. It felt slimy and fun. Elizabeth laughed and laughed. Her tummy did not feel fluttery anymore. The boy sat next to her. He held the frog too.

"Look, he jumps!" said the boy. The frog hopped across the table. Elizabeth clapped her hands. "Let's make him jump again," she said.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Beau sat in his car seat. He was going to Grandma's house. "I can't wait!" said Beau. Daddy said, "Look out the window." The trees bent and shook. "It is windy today," said Daddy.

Beau had a little bag of toys. He looked inside. He saw toy cars. One, two, three cars. Then he saw something yellow. It was long and bendy. "A banana!" said Beau. The banana was hiding with the toy cars. Beau held it up. "You do not go with cars," he said. "You are the odd one out!" He put the banana in the lunch box. It sat by the apple and the crackers.

Then Beau found his book under the seat. "Look, Daddy!" he said. "A book about animals!" Daddy said, "Read it to Grandma when we get there." The car went zoom. Beau hugged his book and smiled.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Myles took him to the park. It was spring, and the flowers were open. The gate was closed, so Grandpa pushed it, and it swung wide.

Myles rode his bike on the path. "My dad rides a big bike," said Myles. "Was Dad always big?"

Grandpa laughed. "No, no. Dad was little once. I know a story about his first bike." Myles stopped pedaling. "Dad was little? Tell me!"

"Dad fell off. Then Dad got up. Then Dad fell off again!" Grandpa said. Myles laughed and laughed.

"I can't see it," said Myles. "Tell it again!"

Grandpa told it again. Dad fell off. Dad got up. This time Myles could see it. Little Dad, on a little bike, wobble, wobble, bump.

"Look at me, Grandpa!" said Myles. He pedaled fast. "I am like little Dad!"

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Nora was at her friend Mia's house. Mia had a tablet on the table. Nora wanted to draw a cat, but she did not know how to make the tablet work. "Can I try?" she asked. Mia's mom said yes.

Mia showed Nora the small button. Nora pressed it once. The screen lit up. Then Mia tapped the little paint picture. A white page opened. Nora put her finger on the screen. She slid it across. A blue line followed her finger. Nora gasped. Her finger moved, and the line moved too. The line went all squiggly. "It looks like a snake," said Nora. She gave it a red tongue and two eyes.

Then it was time for snacks. Nora pressed the button again, and the screen went dark. She put the tablet away in the box, just like Mia's mom showed her. "My snake is in there," said Nora. "Sleeping."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Paisley saw a big blue bus at the park. It was a bookmobile, full of books! She held her mama's hand and they began to walk toward it.

Inside, the shelves went up and up. Paisley ran her fingers over the books. One cover felt rough and bumpy. It was red, with a bear on the front. "This one," said Paisley. "I love this bear."

A kind lady at the desk smiled. "Would you like your own library card?" Paisley stood very tall. The lady typed, and out came a little card with Paisley's name on it. Paisley jumped up and down.

Then the lady scanned the red bear book. Beep! "Now this book is yours to take home," she said. Paisley looked at the card in her hand. The card made the book hers! She hugged the book tight.

"Can I read it at home?" asked Paisley. "All the bear pages?" Mama laughed. "Yes, all of them. Tonight, we will read every page."

Paisley waved to the bookmobile. "Goodbye, books! Goodbye, blue bus!"

She skipped to the car, book under her arm, card in her fist.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Lennon held Mama's hand at the big hall. Little lamps glowed on every table. They looked like tiny stars. Lennon wanted to light one all by herself.

She reached for a match. "No, no," said Auntie Rosa. "Fire is for grown-ups." Lennon's face felt hot. That was the wrong thing to do. She wanted to help anyway.

Mama knelt down beside her. "Pick a lamp for me," said Mama. Lennon looked at the box of lamps. She picked the blue one. It felt smooth in her hands. She gave it to Mama, and Mama lit it with one little match. The flame popped up, small and warm. Lennon clapped her hands.

Auntie Rosa gave the lamp a place on the table. "You sent the blue lamp here," said Mama. "And it glows because of you." Lennon smiled and watched the little flame dance.

Now, everyone needed more lamps. Lennon picked a yellow one for Papa. She picked a green one for Auntie Rosa. Each time, a grown-up did the lighting. Lennon did the picking.

At the end of the night, the whole room was full of light. Lennon looked at her blue lamp. It was still glowing. "That one is mine," she said. "I chose it."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Lucy put on her red hat. "Sunny day," said Mom. "Wear your hat."

At the park, the wind began to whoosh. The trees went swish, swish. Lucy's hat jumped right off her head. "My hat!" she cried. It rolled over the grass. Lucy ran after it, but the wind pushed it again. "It keeps flying away!" she said.

Mom held Lucy's hand. They chased the hat together. The wind blew it near the big tree. Mom picked it up and brushed off the dirt. "This wind is strong," said Mom. "It can blow a hat right off your head." She tucked the hat snug under Lucy's chin. "Hold it with your hand, too."

The wind slowed down. The sun came out warm and bright. Lucy sat on the bench with Mom. She kept her hat on tight. "Nice hat," said a kind old man on the next bench. Lucy smiled. "The wind gave it back," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Hailey sat in the cafe with her mama. She had a paper and a pencil. She wanted to write her name.

She held the pencil in her fist. She pressed hard. The H came out all wiggly. "That looks ugly," she said, and her lip went down.

Mama put her hand over Hailey's hand. She set the pencil on Hailey's middle finger. "Now pinch it," said Mama. Hailey pinched with her thumb and her first finger. The pencil felt light, like a little bird.

She wrote H. Then A. Then I. Then L. Then E. And then Y. "HAILEY!" she said so loud that a man at the next table looked up and smiled.

Mama kissed the top of her head. Hailey wrote her name again. Pinch, rest, write. Pinch, rest, write. Each letter stood up straight, like little trees.

The waiter brought mama's cup, and a cookie for Hailey. On the napkin, Hailey wrote her name one more time. She drew a heart under it and painted the heart red with her pencil.

"Can we take this home?" she asked, holding up the napkin.

"We can," said Mama. "Right after one more HAILEY."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Lily wanted to draw a cat on the big tablet. The tablet sat on the shelf in the computer lab. Lily took it with one hand. The tablet slipped. It wobbled and tipped. "Whoa," said Lily. She caught it just in time.

She tried again. This time she used two hands. One hand on each side. The tablet did not wobble at all. Lily carried it to the table. She walked slow, like an ant carrying a stick.

Now she had to turn it on. She pressed the round button. One, two, three. The screen lit up. She tapped the blue square with her finger. The drawing app opened. Lily made a cat with straight ears and a long tail. Then she made a sun. Then she made a red ball.

Teacher Mia clapped. "Time to put it away," she said. Lily pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She stood up tall. Two hands on the tablet, one on each side. She walked to the shelf. One, two, three, place it down. "All done," said Lily.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story: Sarah went to the store with Grandma. Sarah wanted pancakes on Saturday. "How many days until Saturday?" she asked. "Guess," said Grandma. Sarah held up her little hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven," she said. Seven fingers. Seven days. Sarah giggled. At the store, they saw one big red apple. Then two yellow bananas. Then three cute little oranges in a bag. Sarah put them in the cart one at a time. "Four, five, six," she counted. The cart rolled when she pushed it. Push, roll. That made her laugh. Grandma held up a box. "How many pancakes will we make?" Sarah guessed. "Ten!" she said. "Ten, nine, eight, seven," she counted down. At home they would mix the batter. Grandma would cook. Sarah would watch. "Seven days is a long time," said Sarah. "Yes," said Grandma, "but Saturday always comes." Sarah hugged the apple bag all the way to the car.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Ibrahim sat in his car seat. The car went over a bridge. Below them was a wide river. The water sparkled in the sun.

"I want my juice," said Ibrahim. He reached for the cup. It was far away. His little hand could not get it. He pushed and stretched. His face went hot and cross.

Then he remembered his words. "Daddy, can you help me, please?" he asked. Daddy smiled at him in the mirror. "Of course," said Daddy. He reached back with one hand. He passed the cup to Ibrahim.

"Thank you, Daddy," said Ibrahim. He took a big sip. The juice was cold and sweet. "Sorry I made a grumpy sound," he said. "That's okay," said Daddy.

The car went over another bridge. The river slid under it. Ibrahim waved at the water. "See you, river," he said. He held his cup with both hands. "Can we go to the park early tomorrow?" he asked. "Yes," said Daddy. "Early it is."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Lydia stood at the big baseball diamond. Daddy put a purple hoop on the ground. "Throw the beanbag in," said Daddy.

Lydia threw the beanbag high. She thought it would bounce. She thought it would bounce right into the hoop. But the beanbag came down. Flop. It just sat in the grass. It did not bounce at all. Lydia walked over and picked it up.

"Again," said Lydia. She threw it again, up and up. Flop. It landed in the grass again. Then she threw it low and soft. Flop. It fell right into the hoop. "It went in!" said Lydia. "Good throw," said Daddy. "Bring me the beanbag, please."

Lydia ran and brought it back. Then Daddy rolled her a big ball. "Catch it with both hands," he said. Lydia held out one hand. The ball bumped her fingers and fell. She tried again with one hand. It fell again.

"Both hands," said Daddy. He rolled the ball slowly. Lydia held out both hands. She waited. She waited. The ball came and came. Both hands closed around it. "I caught it!" said Lydia. She hugged the big ball and laughed. "One more time," said Daddy. He rolled the ball again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Charlie ran to the table with muddy hands. She wanted her supper right now!

"Stop!" said Mommy with a laugh. "Look at those paws."

Charlie looked. Her hands were brown and dirty. "Am I a puppy?" she asked.

"A muddy puppy," said Daddy. "Puppies eat from bowls. Do you want a bowl on the floor?"

Charlie giggled. "No! I want a chair."

"Then off to the sink," said Mommy. "We wash our hands before we eat."

Charlie stomped to the sink. Mommy turned on the water. Charlie rubbed and rubbed. The mud went down the drain. Now her hands were pink and clean.

She held them up. "Look, Daddy! No more puppy paws!"

"Smart girl," said Daddy. "Now come and eat."

After supper, Charlie had her bath. The water was warm and bubbly. She washed her tummy and her toes. Then Mommy helped her put on her soft pajamas. They had stars on them.

"I washed my hands before supper," Charlie told her teddy. "And now I am clean all over!"

She climbed into bed. Mommy tucked her in and kissed her nose.

"Tomorrow I will bake cookies with Daddy," Charlie said, "and I will wash my hands first."

"Good plan," said Mommy, turning off the light.

Charlie yugged teddy close. "Night night, muddy puppy," she whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Addison went to the library for story time. She sat on a round rug. It was a big circle.

Miss Jane held up a square book. "Time for a story and a craft," she said. The craft was paper pizza. Addison got red paper and green paper. Then Miss Jane gave her a yellow circle.

Addison wanted to cut the circle. She looked for a corner to start. She turned the paper over. She peeked at the edge. She scratched her head. "Where is the corner?" she said.

Benji next to her laughed. "It ran away," he said. "It did not run," said Addison. "It is not there." She ran her finger all around the paper. Round and round and round. No corner anywhere. "Silly circle," she said. "You have no corners at all."

Miss Jane helped with the scissors, because scissors are for grown-up hands. She cut a red square for cheese and a green triangle for a pepper. Addison glued them on. Benji glued a rectangle for a crust.

"Your pizza looks yummy," said Benji. "Do not eat it," said Addison. "That would be a mean trick on my tummy." Benji giggled so hard he fell over on the round, round rug.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
James sat at the paint table at school. He wanted to paint green grass. But the green paint pot was empty. James looked in the pot. He tipped it upside down. Nothing came out.

"I need green," said James. His teacher, Miss Anne, sat down next to him. "Let me see," she said. She put out a pot of blue paint. Then she put out a pot of yellow paint. "You can try," she said.

James put his brush in the blue paint. He made a blue spot on his paper. Then he put the same brush in the yellow paint. He made a yellow spot on top. James waited. He looked very close. The spot turned green! James smiled big. He dipped his brush again and again. Blue, then yellow. Green, green, green. He painted tall grass all over his paper. "Look, Miss Anne!" he said. "My grass is so green!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Athena had curly hair and a small red chair. She sat in the kitchen with her family. Papa was making soup in the big pot. The soup was hot, so Papa stirred it, not Athena. Athena had her own little cup of cold water. "Cold for me," she said. "Hot for the soup."

Athena wanted to help. Papa said, "You can carry the napkins." The napkins were light. Athena ran fast to the table. Then she walked slow and careful, like a turtle. She put the napkins down, one by one. "I helped!" she said.

Then Athena saw a puddle on the floor. A tiny puddle by the sink. She stomped in it. Splash! Her socks got all wet. "Oh no," said Mama. "Wet socks are cold. You need dry ones." Mama peeled off the wet socks. Athena touched them with one finger. Wet. Then Mama gave her fluffy new socks. Athena squeezed them. Dry and warm.

"Wet socks go here," said Mama. She hung them on the rack. Athena watched the water drip, drip, drip into a bowl. "The socks are crying," Athena whispered. She waved at them. "Bye bye, little tears." The dry fluffy socks waited on her feet, and Athena jumped up and down, soft as a bunny.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Beatrice stood by the blocks at school. She wanted to play with Leo and Mia. But they were busy feeding a teddy bear. Beatrice did not know how to start. She looked at her shoes. She looked at her hands.

Then she took a big breath. "Let's pretend I am the bear's mama," she said. Leo looked up fast. Mia clapped her hands. "Yes! You came home!" said Leo. Just like that, the game began. Beatrice picked up the teddy and hugged him. "My baby," she said softly. "Time for soup."

Mia bent a paper cup and made it a tiny pot. "One spoon, two spoops, three spoons," she counted. Leo wrapped the bear in a red scarf. "Warm blanket, warm baby," he said. Beatrice was happy. She rocked the teddy side to side.

"Let's pretend the bear is sleepy," said Leo. "Let's pretend I sing a song," said Beatrice. She sang a small hum, one note, two notes, three. The teddy closed his button eyes. All the friends whispered, "Shh." Mia set one blanket, then two, then three on top. Then they all tiptoed in a circle around the sleeping bear, hands on lips, giggling like tiny pirates sneaking past a whale.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Lillian had a cold. She caught it from her big brother. Now she was resting at home on the soft couch.

Grandma came over with a big smile. "Would you like some water?" she asked. Lillian shook her head. She did not feel thirsty at all. Her throat was scratchy and her tummy felt funny.

Then Grandma held up a tiny blue cup. It had a plane painted on the side. "This cup is for brave pilots," Grandma said. "Little sips only." Lillian sat up and held the cup. She took one small sip. Then another. The water was cool and fresh.

Soon Lillian felt a bit better. She sat up tall. She wanted to draw a plane just like her cup. Grandma found the crayons and paper. Lillian drew a big plane in the sky. She sipped more water while she drew. "Look, Grandma!" she said. "My plane is flying to the sun." Grandma gave her a gentle hug and one more sip of water in the little blue cup.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
James went to the bank with his dad. It was cold outside. James held his little blue coat in his hands.

"Time to put your coat on," said Dad.

James pushed one arm into one sleeve. Then he looked for the other sleeve. The sleeve was hiding behind his back. James turned around and around. "I can't find it," he said.

A girl named Mia was waiting with her mom. She saw James spinning. "Watch me," said Mia. She laid her coat on the floor. She put her arms in the sleeves. Then she flipped it over her head. The coat was on!

James wondered, could his coat do that too? He laid his coat on the floor. He put his arms in the sleeves. He touched the soft fabric with his fingers. He flipped it over his head. The coat landed on him just right.

"Now the zipper," said Dad. James pulled it up, up, up. Click, it stopped at the top.

"You look good," said Mia. "Your coat has a picture of a bear on it."

James looked down at the bear. "My coat did a flip," he said. "Zip it again, Dad?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Mohamed went to the farmers' market with Dad. They bought a big round loaf of bread. They bought fresh butter in a little dish. A bee tried to fly near the bread. "Go away, bee," said Mohamed. The bee buzzed off to the flowers.

At home, Mohamed wanted to make lunch. "I will spread the butter," he said. He tried. The butter was hard. It would not spread. It made a hole in the bread. "Oh no," said Mohamed. "My bread has a big hole!"

Dad smiled. "Let's put the butter on the counter," he said. They set it down. They washed apples. They sang a silly song about a hammer that went tap, tap, tap. Mohamed's tooth felt a little loose, so he wiggled it with his tongue.

Then Mohamed touched the butter. It was soft now! He spread it, slow and smooth. The bread was all gold and shiny.

"Mohamed made lunch!" said Dad, and he took a big, big bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Rosalie was going on a trip. It was winter, so she wore her red coat. The airport was very busy. So many feet! So many bags!

Then Rosalie saw them. Big planes out the big window! One plane went up, up into the sky. "Look, Mama!" she called. Rosalie wanted to run to the window. She took one step. The crowd was big and fast. Where was Mama's hand? Rosalie reached up and found it. She held on tight.

Mama squeezed her hand. They walked to the window together. The planes were giant, but Rosalie felt tiny next to them. A truck pushed a plane slowly along the ground. "It goes so slow," said Rosalie. A man in a vest waved two big sticks. The plane turned and followed him.

"Where do the planes sleep?" Rosalie asked. Mama smiled and pointed out at the sky. Another plane came down, down, down, soft as a bird.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Kai sat on Grandpa's big red rug. Grandpa had a gift for him. It was a little drum with a happy face.

"Let's sing," said Grandpa. "Clap with me." Grandpa clapped. Clap, clap, clap. Kai clapped too. But Kai did not know the star song words yet. He stopped. His mouth made no sound. That felt like a problem.

Kai waited. He tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. Then he tried a song he knew. "A, B, C, D," he sang. Grandpa's eyes went wide. Grandpa clapped along. Clap, clap, clap. The tune fit! It was the same tune as the star song!

"Now the star words," said Grandpa. He sang. "Twinkle, twinkle." Kai sang too. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." He sang it all by himself.

After the song, Kai patted the drum face. "Was it a naughty drum?" he asked. Grandpa laughed. "It was a good drum. It kept the beat."

Kai clapped and sang again. The goldfish swam in its bowl by the window. Clap, clap, clap went the little drum.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Jaxon woke up at Grandma's house. The sun made a warm line on his blanket. He wanted to go outside and play in the leaves. But first he had to get dressed.

Grandma laid out his clothes. Jaxon pulled on his shirt. He pulled on his pants. Then he sat down with his shoes. He pushed and pushed. His toes felt squished and bumpy inside.

Jaxon knocked on the wall to call Grandma. She came in and smiled. "Try again, sweet boy," she said softly. Jaxon took the shoes off. He looked at his bare feet. He looked at his socks. Then he put the socks on first. His toes felt cozy and warm.

Now the shoes slid right on. Jaxon laughed. He stomped his feet. "Ready!" he said.

He ate his oatmeal by the window. A shy brown rabbit sat near the fence. Grandma filled the tub for a warm bath later. But now it was leaf time.

Jaxon ran outside. He jumped in the leaves with his socks on first, then his shoes. The rabbit hopped away through the golden pile.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Jake went to the library with his mom. He saw a big toy train on the rug. A girl named Mia was already there. She was holding the engine.

"I want the engine," said Jake.

"Me first," said Mia.

They both pulled. The train cars went crash. Blocks fell down. It looked messy on the rug.

Then Mia had an idea. "You can go first," she said. "Then I get a go."

Jake drove the engine around the rug. "Choo choo!" he said. "It's a bee train, going fast!"

Then he stopped. "Your turn now, Mia."

Mia drove the train too. Jake made a tunnel with his arms. The train zoomed through it. They took turns again and again.

The librarian smiled at them. "Time for story time," she said. "Everyone sits in a circle."

Jake sat down next to Mia. She let him hold half of her book.

"I like the bee train," said Jake.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Mason was at Grandma's house. He could not find his monkey. "Where did you go, monkey?" he asked.

Mason looked under the big chair. No monkey. He looked in the toy box. One car, two blocks, three balls. No monkey. Grandpa said, "Let's look in the garden."

They looked by the flowers. They looked by the swing. No monkey. Then Mason saw something. "Spotted fur!" he said. The monkey was in the green bush.

"Grandma, who found him?" asked Mason.

"The bus driver did," said Grandma. "He knocked on the door. He saw the tag on the monkey."

Mason looked at the tag. It had his name. M-A-S-O-N. The bus driver read the name. Then he brought the monkey to Mason.

"What a good tag," said Mason. "It says my name!"

Later, Mason took a sticker and a pen. He asked Grandma to help. She wrote his name on the tag. Mason held the tag up high.

"Now everyone knows," said Mason. "This monkey is mine!"

He hugged the monkey tight. "Hello, monkey. Hello, tag."

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Brooklyn went to the library with her mama. She wanted to write her name. She found a basket of bumpy letter cards. Each card had a big letter on it. Brooklyn picked up the letter B. "B says buh," she said. The letter A said "ah." The letter K said "kuh."

Brooklyn got a crayon and paper. She tried to write K. She made the lines go the wrong way. "Oh no," she said. "That looks bad." She tried again. The K was still wrong. Her mouth turned down.

Then Mama sat close by her. "Try the bumpy card," Mama said softly. Brooklyn put her finger on the bumpy K. She traced the shape. Down the tall line. Then the little arm. Then the other arm. The bumps tickled her finger. She traced it again and again.

Now Brooklyn picked up her crayon. She drew the K. The tall line went down. The arms went out. The K was right! Brooklyn held the paper up high. The lamp made her letters shine. "Look, Mama! Brooklyn!" She traced the K one more time, just to feel the bumps. "Kuh, kuh, Brooklyn," she said.

story:
Emile wants to read a book all by himself. He finds a thick red book on the rug. He opens it near the cover, like always. He turns the pages from front to back. "Am I doing it right?" he asks. Miss Ada smiles. "Look at the pictures. Do they tell you a story?"

Then his friend Noa comes over. She has a little blue flag on her bag. She holds up her own book. "This one opens the other way," she says. Emile looks. The book opens from the left side. The pages turn the other way. "Why does it do that?" he asks. "It is in Hebrew," Noa says. "We read it from right to left."

Emile tries it. He opens her book the new way. He turns the pages with care. The pictures flow like a little river. Then he takes his red book again. He finds the first page. He puts his finger under a word. The word says "cat", and the picture shows a cat. Emile laughs and turns to Noa. "Your book is a book too, just turned around," he says.

story:
Ava sat at the dinner table. She drank warm milk from her cup. "Milk comes from a cow," said Daddy. Ava giggled. A big cow! Moo!

After dinner, Ava begged, "Can I stay up late? Please, please?" Outside, the sky was stormy and dark. "No, sweet pea," said Mommy. "It is bedtime." Ava got a warm bath. The water smelled like soap. She put on her soft pajamas. She got kisses and went to sleep.

In the morning, Ava woke up with stretchy arms. "I feel big!" she said. She ran to her blocks. She stacked them tall, so tall. She danced with her bear. "Wow," said Ava. "I slept, and now I can play!" She clapped her hands. "Bedtime again tonight?" she asked Mommy. Mommy smiled and nodded.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Blake ran into Mia's house. Music was playing in the big room!

"Listen!" said Mia. "We will sing a song. My mom will count first."

Blake was so excited. She opened her mouth to sing. "Twinkle, twin..."

"Wait," said Mia. "Not yet! You will lose your place. Wait for the count."

Blake closed her mouth. She waited. Her hands sat still.

Mia's mom stood up tall. "One, two, three, four!" she said.

"Now!" cried Mia. Both girls sang at the same time. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star!"

Blake clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. Her claps fit right on the beat, just like the song!

"You did it!" said Mia.

Then came the small surprise. Mia's mom clapped too. Clap, clap, clap! Even the dog barked, woof, woof, woof.

"This is easy!" said Blake. She sang it again. "One, two, three, four," she counted all by herself.

"Twinkle, twinkle, little star!"

story:
Felix wanted to write Grandpa a note. He took a pencil and wrote his letters. He wrote big and small, all in a row. "This says come play with me," he said.

Grandpa looked at the note. He shook his head. "I see letters," he said. "But the words are all squished." Felix looked at his paper. All his letters were holding hands in one long line. Then Grandpa held up a book. He turned the pages from the front to the back. Felix looked close. The words had little gaps between them. Was that why Grandpa could read them?

Felix tapped his pencil. He drew a small space after each word. "Now can you read it?" he asked. Grandpa smiled big. "Come play with me," he read out loud. Felix clapped. "The spaces did it!" he said.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Florence went to the library with Dad. She wanted a book about a mouse. She found one with a tiny gray mouse on the cover.

"Please read it," she said. Dad opened the front of the book. He read the first page. Then the next page. He pointed at the little black marks under the picture. "I read these words," he said. Florence touched the marks with her finger. Dad's voice had come from them!

One page had only a picture. The mouse looked at a big cheese. "Read this one!" said Florence. Dad turned the page slowly. "There are no words here," he said. "Nothing to read." Florence looked hard. The page was empty of marks.

She turned back to a page with words. Dad read them. The mouse began to move to the cheese. Florence laughed.

She held the book herself. She started at the front. She turned each page one by one. "This is a special book," she said. Dad smiled and read the words again.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Hudson sat at the kitchen table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. He had paper and a brush. But the orange paint jar was empty. Hudson looked and looked. No orange anywhere.

He found red paint. He found yellow paint. Hudson sighed. Then he dipped his brush in red. He put red on the paper. He dipped his brush in yellow. He put yellow on top of the red. He swirled it around. The paint turned orange! Hudson gasped. His pumpkin was orange now.

Mom set a snack beside him. It was salty crackers. Hudson munched one. He painted a big pumpkin. Then he painted a little bear next to it. "The bear can sleep by the pumpkin," Hudson said. He put down his brush and smiled.

story:
Isla went to the pharmacy with Mama. There was a little sink by the counter. It had pink soap and a paper towel holder. A sign showed a fox washing its paws. Isla wanted to wash her hands there too.

Mama bought some medicine. Then she said, "Isla, it is almost snack time." Isla held up her hands. "My hands aren't dirty!" she said. They looked clean and smooth. Mama turned on the water anyway. It felt cool and bubbly. Isla pumped the pink soap. It smelled like flowers.

"Now we sing," said Mama. They sang a little song about a fox. Isla rubbed the soap hard between her fingers. Bubbles went pop, pop, pop. She counted to twenty with Mama. Then she dried her hands on the paper towel. At home, Isla ate her crackers. "Good washing," said Mama. Isla looked at her clean hands and smiled.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Eli sat on his bed. He had a big red book. He wanted to know what the dog in the picture was doing. But the pages had little black marks too. They were words.

Eli put his finger at the right side of the page. He moved it that way. The words felt like a big jumble. He tried again. His finger ran into the edge of the book. "Hmm," said Eli.

Mom came in and sat down. "Read with me," she said. She opened the book at the front. "This part comes first," she said. Then she put her finger at the left side of the page. Her finger slid to the right. The words flowed out like a little river. "The dog can jump," Mom read.

Eli looked. Yes! The dog was jumping over a pot in the picture. Eli put his finger on the left side. He slid it to the right. "The pot fell down," he said. Mom smiled and clapped.

Eli turned the page himself. He started on the left again. "Read it to me," he said, and patted the bed.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Eleanor turned four today. There were balloons on the door. Grandma was baking bread. Dad was stirring something sweet.

Then the door opened. Friends came in with presents. Big ones and small ones!

Eleanor grabbed the first box. She pulled off the paper fast. Inside was a red truck with a strong wheel that spun round and round. Leo had brought it.

She dropped it and ran to the next box. That one had a pretend kitchen with tiny pots. She hugged the pots to her chest.

Then she stopped. Leo was standing quietly by the wall. He looked down at his shoes.

Eleanor ran back to him. She held up the red truck. "Thank you, Leo!" she said.

Leo smiled a big smile. "You can spin the wheel again," he said. "Watch me!"

He pushed the truck across the floor. The wheel spun fast, all the way to the cake.
